For expressions found in the problem statement:
\framebox{α∈ℱ,  α(m)=0 for m<0, m>8}
\[
(S_nα)⋆β=\sum_{t∈ℤ}α(t+n)β(t)=1\;(n=k,l),\;0\text{ otherwise.}
\]

**Key insight – polynomial language**  
Identify a function α with the integer polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}α(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x] .
\]

Similarly let \(B'(x)=\sum_{j}β'(j)x^{j}\) where \(β'(j)=β(-j)\).  
Then  

\[
(S_nα)⋆β=\sum_iα(i)β(i-n)=\sum_iα(i)β'(n-i)=(A*B')(n),
\]

i.e. the convolution of the coefficient sequences, which is exactly the coefficient of \(x^{n}\) in the product \(A(x)B'(x)\).

Thus the condition becomes  

\[
A(x)B'(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{k}(1+x^{D}),\qquad D=|l-k|>0 .
\]

Multiplying the whole equation by \(x^{-k}\) (absorbing the factor \(x^{k}\) into \(B'\)) we obtain  

\[
A(x)C(x)=1+x^{D},
\]

with \(C(x)=x^{k}B'(x)\in\mathbb Z[x]\).  
Hence **α is shifty iff its polynomial A(x) divides a binomial \(1+x^{D}\) for some \(D>0\).**

**Factorisation of \(1+x^{D}\)**  
Over \(\mathbb Z[x]\),

\[
1+x^{D}= \frac{x^{2D}-1}{x^{D}-1}
      =\prod_{\substack{d\mid2D\\ d\not\mid D}}\Phi_{d}(x),
\]

where \(\Phi_{d}\) is the \(d\)-th cyclotomic polynomial.  
All indices \(d\) occurring are **even**, because \(d\mid2D\) but \(d\nmid D\) forces a factor 2.  
Consequently any divisor of \(1+x^{D}\) is a product (with sign) of distinct cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{d}\) with **even** \(d\).

**Degree restriction**  
Since α must vanish for \(m>8\), we need \(\deg A\le8\).  
Thus we only consider even \(d\) with \(\varphi(d)\le8\) (φ = Euler totient).  
A quick computation gives

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
d & \varphi(d)\\\hline
2&1\\4&2\\6&2\\8&4\\10&4\\12&4\\14&6\\16&8\\18&6\\20&8\\24&8\\30&8
\end{array}
\]

These 12 cyclotomic polynomials are the only possible irreducible factors.

**Counting admissible products**  
Any admissible A(x) is a product of a subset of the above 12 polynomials, each used at most once, with total degree ≤8.  
The empty subset gives the constant polynomial 1 (and with sign –1).  

Enumerating all subsets whose degree‑sum ≤8 yields **44** distinct polynomials (including the constant 1).  
Since we may also multiply by –1, each gives a distinct α, so the total number of shifty functions is  

\[
{answer = 2\times44=88}.
\]

**Pitfalls to avoid**  
- Do not forget the sign factor: both A and –A are valid (they give different α).  
- Ensure that every subset’s total degree ≤8; a single factor of degree >8 is not allowed.  
- Verify that any chosen subset can indeed be realized as a divisor of some \(1+x^{D}\); this holds because all even‑indexed cyclotomics can be simultaneously accommodated by choosing \(D\) with a 2‑adic exponent one less than the smallest among the factors and odd part equal to the lcm of their odd parts.  
- No other integer polynomials (with coefficients beyond ±1) can divide a binomial \(1+x^{D}\); all such divisors are products of the listed cyclotomics.  

Thus the answer is **88** shifty functions.

For expressions found in the problem statement:
\framebox{α∈ℱ is “shifty’’ ⇔ ∃β∈ℱ, k≠ℓ∈ℤ such that  
  Sₙ(α)⋆β = 1 for n∈{k,ℓ} and 0 otherwise.}

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Key insight – translate to polynomials**

Write the finitely‑supported integer function α as a polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x] .
\]

For β define the Laurent polynomial  

\[
C(x)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\beta(j)x^{j}\in\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}].
\]

Then  

\[
S_{n}(\alpha)\star\beta=\sum_{t}\alpha(t+n)\beta(t)
\]

is exactly the coefficient of \(x^{\,n}\) in the product \(A(x)C(x)\).  
Hence the condition on α is equivalent to

\[
A(x)C(x)=x^{k}+x^{\ell}=x^{\ell}\bigl(1+x^{d}\bigr),\qquad d=|k-\ell|>0 .
\tag{1}
\]

Thus **α is shifty iff its polynomial A(x) divides a binomial \(x^{d}+1\) in the Laurent ring \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\).**  
Since a monomial factor \(x^{\ell}\) can be absorbed into C(x), (1) is equivalent to

\[
x^{-p}A(x)\mid x^{d}+1\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z[x],
\]

for some integer \(p\ge0\).  Consequently  

\[
A(x)=x^{p}B(x),\qquad B(x)\mid x^{d}+1\text{ in }\mathbb Z[x],
\tag{2}
\]

with \(\deg A\le8\) (because α(m)=0 for m<0, m>8).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Cyclotomic factorisation**

\(x^{d}+1=\displaystyle\prod_{\substack{m\mid2d\\ m\nmid d}}\Phi_{m}(x)\),

where \(\Phi_{m}\) is the \(m\)-th cyclotomic polynomial.  
All factors are distinct and each \(\Phi_{m}\) is monic.  
Hence any divisor \(B\) of some \(x^{d}+1\) is a product of a *subset* of those cyclotomic factors.

Only even‑indexed cyclotomic polynomials can appear (odd‑indexed ones never divide \(x^{d}+1\)).  
Moreover we need \(\deg B\le8\).  The even‑indexed cyclotomic polynomials with degree ≤8 are:

| m | \(\Phi_{m}(x)\) | deg |
|---|----------------|-----|
| 2 | \(x+1\) | 1 |
| 4 | \(x^{2}+1\) | 2 |
| 6 | \(x^{2}-x+1\) | 2 |
| 8 | \(x^{4}+1\) | 4 |
|10 | \(x^{4}-x^{3}+x^{2}-x+1\) | 4 |
|12 | \(x^{4}-x^{2}+1\) | 4 |
|14 | \(x^{6}-x^{5}+x^{4}-x^{3}+x^{2}-x+1\) | 6 |
|16 | \(x^{8}+1\) | 8 |
|18 | \(x^{6}-x^{3}+1\) | 6 |
|20 | \(x^{8}-x^{6}+x^{4}-x^{2}+1\) | 8 |
|24 | \(x^{8}-x^{4}+1\) | 8 |
|30 | \(x^{8}+x^{7}-x^{5}-x^{4}-x^{3}+x+1\) | 8 |

(Only the degrees are needed for counting.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Counting admissible B**

A monic divisor \(B\) is any product of a *subset* of the 12 cyclotomics above whose total degree ≤8.  
Enumerating all subsets gives **44** distinct monic polynomials \(B\) (including the empty product \(B=1\)).  

For each such \(B\) we may also take its negative \(-B\) (since \((-B)(-C)=x^{d}+1\) as well).  Thus each \(B\) yields **2** choices of sign.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Shifts**

If \(B\) has degree \(d_B\), then in (2) we may choose any shift exponent \(p\) with  

\[
0\le p\le 8-d_B .
\]

The shift corresponds to multiplying by \(x^{p}\), i.e. moving the support of α to start at index \(p\).  
There are \(9-d_B\) possible values of \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Total number of shifty functions**

Summing over all admissible \(B\):

\[
\#\text{shifty}= \sum_{B} 2\,(9-\deg B)
               = 2\sum_{B}(9-\deg B)
               = 266 .
\]

(Computed by brute‑force enumeration of the 44 subsets.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Pitfalls to avoid**

* Forgetting that β may be a Laurent polynomial, i.e. its support can be on negative indices; this is why we work in \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\) and allow a monomial factor to be absorbed into β.
* Assuming only monic divisors matter – the sign ± also yields distinct α, so multiply the count by 2.
* Over‑counting: different pairs \((d,k,\ell)\) can give the same α; the polynomial viewpoint avoids this.
* Missing cyclotomic factors of degree ≤8; the list above is exhaustive (checked up to 1000, and theory shows only the 12 even m with φ(m)≤8).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Result**

\[
{answer = 266}
\]

For expressions found in the problem statement:
\framebox{α∈ℱ is “shifty’’ ⇔ ∃β∈ℱ, k≠l∈ℤ such that  
  Sₙ(α)⋆β = 1 for n∈{k,l} and 0 otherwise.}

---

### 1.  Reformulation as a convolution/divisibility problem  

Write α,β as integer‑valued sequences with finite support.  
\(S_n(α)⋆β =\sum_t α(t+n)β(t)=\sum_j α(j)β(j-n)\).  

Define the Laurent polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{j}α(j)x^{j},\qquad B(x)=\sum_{j}β(j)x^{j}.
\]

Then the above sum is the coefficient of \(x^{n}\) in the product \(A(x)B(x)\).  
Hence the condition is

\[
A(x)B(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{k}(1+x^{d}),\qquad d=l-k\neq0 .
\]

Since a monomial \(x^{k}\) is a unit in the Laurent ring \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\), the existence of β is equivalent to

\[
A(x)\mid 1+x^{d}\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}].
\]

Thus a shifty α is exactly a (primitive) divisor of some polynomial \(1+x^{d}\), up to a monomial factor.

---

### 2.  Divisors of \(1+x^{d}\)

Factorisation over ℤ:

\[
x^{d}+1=\prod_{\substack{e\mid 2d\\ e\nmid d}}\Phi_{e}(x),
\]

where \(\Phi_{e}\) is the e‑th cyclotomic polynomial.  
The indices that appear are precisely the even numbers with exactly one factor 2:
\(e=2q\) where \(q\) is odd and \(q\mid d\).  
Hence any divisor of \(1+x^{d}\) is a product of a **subset** of the cyclotomic polynomials

\[
\Phi_{2q}(x),\qquad q\text{ odd},\;q\mid d .
\]

Only those with degree ≤8 can occur because α is supported in \([0,8]\).  
Since \(\deg\Phi_{2q}=\varphi(q)\) (Euler’s totient), we need odd \(q\) with \(\varphi(q)\le8\).

The odd \(q\) satisfying this are  

\[
q\in\{1,3,5,7,9,15\},
\]

giving the cyclotomics  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{2}&=x+1\;(deg=1),\\
\Phi_{6}&=x^{2}-x+1\;(deg=2),\\
\Phi_{10}&=x^{4}-x^{3}+x^{2}-x+1\;(deg=4),\\
\Phi_{14}&=x^{6}-x^{5}+x^{4}-x^{3}+x^{2}-x+1\;(deg=6),\\
\Phi_{18}&=x^{6}-x^{3}+1\;(deg=6),\\
\Phi_{30}&=x^{8}+x^{7}-x^{5}-x^{4}-x^{3}+x+1\;(deg=8).
\end{aligned}
\]

All have constant term 1, so any product of a subset of them is primitive and divides some \(1+x^{d}\) (take \(d\) the l.c.m. of the chosen odd \(q\)’s).

---

### 3.  Form of all shifty α  

Let \(p(x)=\prod_{q\in S}\Phi_{2q}(x)\) for a subset \(S\subseteq\{1,3,5,7,9,15\}\) (empty product gives \(p=1\)).  
Let \(c\ge0\) be an integer shift.  
Then

\[
{answer = A(x)=\pm x^{c}\,p(x)}
\]

has degree \(\deg A = c+\deg p\le8\); its support lies in \([0,8]\).  
Conversely, any shifty α must be of this form, because any divisor of \(1+x^{d}\) is square‑free and consists exactly of those cyclotomics.

Thus counting shifty functions reduces to counting triples \((S,c,\pm)\) with  

\[
c\ge0,\qquad c+\deg p\le8 .
\]

---

### 4.  Counting  

For each subset \(S\) compute \(\deg p=\sum_{q\in S}\varphi(q)\) (using \(\varphi(1)=1,\varphi(3)=2,\varphi(5)=4,\varphi(7)=6,\varphi(9)=6,\varphi(15)=8\)).  
If \(\deg p\le8\) then admissible shifts are \(c=0,1,\dots,8-\deg p\) – a total of \(8-\deg p+1\) choices.  
Each choice yields two signs (±).  

Summing over all subsets:

```python
qs = [1,3,5,7,9,15]
phi = {1:1,3:2,5:4,7:6,9:6,15:8}
total = 0
for S in powerset(qs):
    deg = sum(phi[q] for q in S)
    if deg <= 8:
        total += (8 - deg + 1) * 2
```

The result is **114**.

---

### 5.  Pitfalls to avoid  

* Forgetting that cyclotomic factors appear only with exponent 1 (1 + xᵈ is square‑free).  
* Ignoring the monomial unit factor; the shift \(c\) must be counted.  
* Assuming coefficients can be arbitrary; the divisor condition forces the content of α to be 1 (primitive).  
* Over‑counting: different subsets give distinct polynomials because cyclotomics are irreducible and pairwise distinct.

---

**Answer:** There are **114** shifty functions in ℱ.

For expressions found in the problem statement:
\framebox{ \(\displaystyle 
\alpha\star\beta =\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\alpha(n)\beta(n),\qquad 
S_n(\alpha)(t)=\alpha(t+n)\)}  

the condition  

\[
S_n(\alpha)\star\beta=
\begin{cases}
1&n\in\{k,l\}\\[2mm]
0&\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

is exactly the **cross‑correlation** of the two integer sequences \(\alpha,\beta\).  
Writing the sequences as polynomials  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i\ge0}\alpha(i)x^{i},\qquad 
B(x)=\sum_{j\ge0}\beta(j)x^{j},
\]

the correlation (1) becomes the product  

\[
A(x)\,B(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}. \tag{2}
\]

Thus a function \(\alpha\) is *shifty* iff its polynomial \(A(x)\) (with
\(\deg A\le8\) because \(\alpha(m)=0\) for \(m<0,\,m>8\)) divides a
binomial \(x^{b}+1\) for some integer \(b\ge1\).  
Indeed, if \(A\mid(x^{b}+1)\) we can take \(k=0,\;l=b\) and
\(B(x)=(x^{b}+1)/A(x)\); then (2) holds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Divisors of \(x^{b}+1\)

Factorisation over \(\mathbb Z[x]\) gives  

\[
x^{b}+1=\prod_{\substack{d\mid2b\\ d\not\mid b}}\Phi_{d}(x),
\]

where \(\Phi_{d}\) is the \(d\)-th cyclotomic polynomial.
If \(b=2^{s}m\;(m\text{ odd})\) then the indices that appear are  

\[
d=2^{s+1}q\qquad(q\mid m,\;q\text{ odd}).
\]

Hence **every divisor of a binomial \(x^{b}+1\) is a product of cyclotomic
polynomials whose indices have the same 2‑adic exponent**.  
Conversely, any product of cyclotomics \(\Phi_{2^{r}q}\) (with a fixed
\(r\ge1\) and odd \(q\)) divides \(x^{\,2^{\,r-1}m}+1\) where
\(m\) is a common multiple of the chosen odd \(q\)’s.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  What can appear inside the interval \([0,8]\)?

Write a divisor as  

\[
A(x)=\pm x^{t}\prod_{q\in S}\Phi_{2^{r}q}(x),\qquad t\ge0,
\tag{3}
\]

where all \(q\) are odd, the set \(S\) is finite and all indices share the
same \(r\ge1\).  
The degree of \(\Phi_{2^{r}q}\) is \(\varphi(2^{r}q)=2^{\,r-1}\varphi(q)\);
hence  

\[
\deg A = t+2^{\,r-1}\sum_{q\in S}\varphi(q)\le8. \tag{4}
\]

Only odd numbers with \(\varphi(q)\le8\) can occur; they are  

\[
q\in\{1,3,5,7,9,15\},\qquad
\varphi(q)=1,2,4,6,6,8 .
\]

For each \(r\) we must have  

\[
\sum_{q\in S}\varphi(q)\le L_r,\qquad 
L_r=\Big\lfloor\frac{8}{2^{\,r-1}}\Big\rfloor .
\]

Thus  

| \(r\) | weight \(2^{r-1}\) | \(L_r\) |
|------|-------------------|--------|
| 1    | 1                 | 8 |
| 2    | 2                 | 4 |
| 3    | 4                 | 2 |
| 4    | 8                 | 1 |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Enumerating all possibilities

For each \(r=1,2,3,4\)

* list all subsets \(S\) of the six odd numbers above whose
  \(\sum\varphi(q)\le L_r\);
* form the product \(D(x)=\prod_{q\in S}\Phi_{2^{r}q}(x)\);
* for every shift \(t=0,\dots,8-\deg D\) and for both signs \(\pm\),
  set \(A(x)=\pm x^{t}D(x)\).

Two different triples \((r,S,t,\pm)\) never give the same polynomial
except for the trivial case \(D=1\) (the empty set), which is counted only
once.  Storing the coefficient vectors \((\alpha(0),\dots,\alpha(8))\) in a
set yields all distinct shifty functions.
